inline.s: The Master escorted westward, the great work done; seeking the Way eastward, the true path won.

blocks.text: 16. The Three Elders of Dawei Village Talk of Old Times; One Word at the Jin'an Bridge Points Out the Lost Path

inline.s: Turn a thousand times and still the heart is a boat that stays unmoved; but when the wind rolls and the waves heave, the craft is hard to hold.
Face the rushing current, hold fast the rudder and the helm; with a light sail all the way, glide at last to the shore.

Qiu Changchun and his elder fellow disciples came to Dawei Village in Xianyang and found the houses in ruins and the hamlet desolate. Three old men were seated at the gateway of a shrine. Changchun stepped forward and made a deep bow, then asked the way to the dwelling of the Filial-and-Incorrupt Gentleman Wang. One of the elders, whose beard and hair were all white, said, “You ask for the residence of Wang the Filial and Incorrupt — can you have some connexion with him?” Qiu Changchun replied, “He was our master. He spread the Way in Shandong and, his feathered transformation accomplished, ascended as a transcendent. The several of us have escorted his spirit-coffin back and yesterday sought ground beneath the Southern Mountain to lay him to rest. Now we were to return to Shandong, so we have come to ask after his household. Are they safe and well?”

At these words the old man sighed and said, “Your master is my elder cousin of the same clan. I am third in seniority, and so people call me Wang San Lao. Ever since my cousin left home, his wife née Zhou fretted herself into illness and died of it. His son Qiulang went off with his father-in-law, returning once every half year or so, so that now there is no one in the household.” Changchun asked, “How has the village fallen into such ruin?” Wang San Lao sighed again and said, “After my cousin left, there was no one in the village to take charge of affairs; each man looked only to himself. When matters arose, there was no one to step forward and set them in order, so men simply let themselves be dragged along by others. Thus things grew worse and worse, the more cunning the poorer, and in the end the village was ruined. Afterwards, when folk heard the Filial and Incorrupt had become a transcendent, they all said he had carried off the vital spirit of the land and lightly laid the blame upon him.”

Changchun asked again, “How do you know he became a transcendent?” Wang San Lao pointed to the shrine and said, “This is the temple that the several villages south and north built for him; go in and look for yourselves.” Changchun and his elder fellow disciples entered the hall and saw the Master's image enshrined above, as lifelike as in life; and they all went up together and bowed. They saw the four characters “Zhenghu Renhao” written on a framed plaque, while the couplet flanking it read: “He displayed his art in Xianyang, holding wine in his mouth and spraying it out (
xùn
, that is, to take liquid into the mouth and spurt it forth) to quench the fire; he poured his gracious light upon his homeland and issued talismans to drive off the plague.”

Qiu, Liu and the rest had read it through, yet did not understand its meaning, so they asked the three elders how he had driven off the plague and quenched the fire. San Lao said, “That year plague was rampant in our region and spread heavily, so that every soul was terrified. Suddenly there appeared a Daoist priest in yellow garments, who wrote efficacious talismans in vermilion and distributed them throughout the villages, never taking a single coin. Whoever obtained one of these talismans and pasted it on the door found the plague at once dissipated. Again, folk said that a fire broke out in the market of Xianyang and caught the people's houses, and that none could put it out. They saw a Daoist, also in a yellow robe, come out of a tavern with a half-cup of wine held aloft in his hand. He took a sip and sprayed it toward the fire, and the fire went out of itself. The townsfolk, moved by his deed in saving them from the blaze, all came to ask his name. He answered, “Three horizontals end-to-end is my surname; three scholars with open mouths make my name.” Having spoken, he drifted away and in the twinkling of an eye was gone. Afterwards some wisehead unravelled the two phrases: three horizontals end-to-end spell “Wang”! Three scholars with mouths spell “Zhe”! They said he must be Wang Zhe. This talk reached our village, and only then did we know he had become a transcendent. We had a cousin of our own clan, known as Mama Wang, who at her dying breath also said, “Uncle, the Filial and Incorrupt, dressed in yellow, has come to take me away.” For this reason the villages south and north, mindful of the grace of his protection, have taken the lead in building this shrine to repay his virtue. On the left wall hangs a wooden board recording the deed; one look and you will understand.”
Liu, Qiu and the others went together below the board, and looking up, read its inscription, which said:

It has long been heard that those who labour for the state are honoured with sacrifice, and those who render merit to the people are honoured with sacrifice. Our worthy Grandfather Wang, whose given name was Zhe, was a man of the extraordinary. In youth he studied letters; in maturity he practised the martial arts. After he was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt, he feigned illness so that he could not speak. No one could fathom his movements; for twelve years he nourished his ailment without once stepping out to gaze afar. One day he vanished, and none knew whither he had gone. Search was made in all directions, yet no trace of him was found. Afterwards plague arose, and the gentleman distributed talismans to save the folk, preserving not a few lives, so that the whole countryside shared in his grace. Again, in the market of Xianyang he spat wine to extinguish a fire and left his name behind in a riddle. He guided his widowed sister-in-law to ascend to heaven and bestowed much fortune on the villagers. Since the gentleman did not forget his own village, how could the villagers turn their backs upon him! Moreover, having the merits of driving away plague and quenching fire, it is fitting that the people should offer him sacrifice. Therefore we have gathered the villagers in common deliberation and taken the lead in building this hall and erecting his image, that at the seasons of the year we may offer sacrifice to repay his toil. Thus we say this.”

Qiu and Liu, having read it, sighed and said, “How unfathomable is the Master's divine foresight, how inexhaustible his transformations — far beyond what we can comprehend!” Then they saw Wang San Lao whisper something into the ear of a young servant; no one knew what words he spoke, but the boy nodded and went off. Before long he returned with a farmhand, carrying a woven basket — pronounced
lǒng
— filled with cakes and the like, and set it before the fellow seekers to enjoy.

Liu and Qiu had no sooner begun to speak a word of thanks when San Lao said, “I have put you to the trouble of escorting my cousin's spirit-coffin back to his homeland and of coming again to inquire after his family. I have nothing fine to offer, only a plain meal, which hardly deserves your thanks.” Seeing him speak thus, Qiu and Liu sat down to eat. That night they lodged in the shrine, and many came to call on them. At daybreak the next morning food was sent from seven or eight quarters. How could their few fellow seekers eat so much? They took only a little from each household, to acknowledge its kindness.

Liu Changsheng consulted with the fellow seekers: they took the more than ten taels of travelling silver that Ma Danyang had given them and handed it to San Lao, to be used for repairing the Master's shrine. All the fellow seekers approved of this. Thereupon they gave the silver to San Lao and explained their purpose. Wang San Lao received it, and Qiu, Liu and the others took their leave and set out.

Leaving Dawei Village, they went on more than ten li to a great tree and sat down to rest awhile. Tan Changzhen said, “Escorting the Master westward, we have finished the great matter. If we were to go on to Shandong, it would be only to eat a few of Elder Brother Ma's meals and spend a little of his money. As the saying goes, “No feast in the world does not break up.” It is also said, “The Way does not cling to feeling; to cling to feeling is not the Way.” If we travel so long together, shall we not be seen as “three making a company, five forming a faction,” which only stirs gossip and is greatly to our inconvenience? Better that each go his own way, and so gain his freedom.” Wang, Hao and the others said, “What Elder Brother says is right.” So Liu Changsheng went off to the southeast, Wang Yuyang toward the southwest, Tan Changzhen headed south, and She Taigu east. Qiu Changchun, seeing the several roads all taken, found nowhere to go, and there in the Shaanxi region he begged for his keep and practised with a firm resolve. Of this we will say nothing for now.

Now of She Taigu alone it is told that he wandered into the region of Jin and saw a stone bridge of some eight or nine arches. Beneath it the foundations were bedrock born of the earth, and whenever autumn and winter came and the river ran dry, the famished refugees who had fled calamity would shelter there. She Taigu saw that under the bridge it was very clean, and since it was just then the season of low water, he sat in meditation beneath it. At first no one knew he was there, and so it was quiet. But by and by people gradually came to know of it, and this drew entanglements upon him. The nearby residents, moved that he sat in meditation from morning to night, recognised him for a man of practice, and so often brought him steamed buns and flat cakes. How could he eat so much? What remained he piled before him. The sparrows and crows seized upon it, each pecking a scrap and flying up, only to let the morsel fall into the water or drop onto the road. When the little children saw it, they picked it up and ate. Following the track and catching at the shadow, they came under the bridge and played before Taigu. Seeing him sit motionless, like a figure moulded of clay or carved from wood, the children, once grown familiar, took him for a bodhisattva and set about building him a shrine. They gathered stones and broken tiles and stacked them on both sides for walls, broke off branches to serve as beams, and pulled grass to cover it with. Each day after eating at home they would call one another and troop down under the bridge, where they kowtowed and made obeisance to She Taigu, laughing and shouting and raising an endless racket. She Taigu was a man of deep forbearance; he paid it no mind, and let them tumble about, squabble, and leap as they would, never once attending to them. This too may be counted as finding stillness amid clamour, and was not without benefit.

One day the nearby village held a Guanyin Lotus-Seat festival. The little children had all gone to watch it, and the place was very quiet. She Taigu saw a man under the bridge polishing a brick: he would rub it a while, then hold it up to his face to look; look, then rub; rub, then look again; and so on some dozens of times, until he had worn one brick away, whereupon he took up a second to polish. Taigu, seeing him toil half the day, thought he meant to grind the brick into some vessel. Now that he saw the man reduce the brick to mud to no purpose whatever, and then begin polishing a second, he feared the man was wasting his labour and was minded to point the way for him. So he asked the brick-polisher, “In polishing this brick, do you mean to make some vessel of it?” The man answered, “Just so.” She Taigu then said to him, “If you would make a vessel, you must first hold a set purpose in mind: either pare away the high and smooth the low, or take what is square and bring it to round. Only by following the compass and the square can you achieve a fine result. Now you follow no measure but grind at random — how can you succeed! Let me ask you, in the end what vessel are you making?” The man answered, “I thought to polish the brick bright and make a mirror of it, that morning and evening I might look upon my face.” At this She Taigu laughed and said, “A brick is but kiln-fired clay, neither bronze nor iron; how can it be polished bright? Are you not throwing away your labour?” The man laughed heartily and said, “By your own reasoning, even as my brick cannot be ground into a mirror, so your sitting — how can it bring you to transcendence? Your dry, fruitless sitting is no different from my polishing of a brick.” At these words She Taigu gave a violent start! He hastily rose and hurried forward, wishing to ask instruction; but the man drifted away and he could not speak with him. She Taigu knew that an extraordinary being had come to point out that dry sitting was no different. He packed his gear, left the Jin'an Bridge, and set out for the region of You and Yan (the northern part of present-day Hebei and the region of Liaoning). There is a poem lamenting it:
To grind a brick, how vain the toil must be; to sit in lone seclusion, breath runs dry.
Both alike are labours fruitlessly; one word of counsel clears the mazed eye.

Leaving aside She Taigu's journey north, we go on to tell of Changzhen's journey south. One day he reached the region of Suizhou (in the north of present-day Hubei). The day was drawing to a close, and there was neither old temple nor cool pavilion, nor any inn to take in a traveller. He saw by the roadside a great manor with many rooms, and meant to go and ask lodging for the night, and in the course of it to beg a little vegetarian fare. Just as he was approaching the gate, a man came out from within, looking like the manager of the estate. This man was surnamed Gu, named Zucheng, with the style name Yufeng. In former years he too had been fond of the Way, but because idle fellow seekers had played at being immortals to swindle his money, and he had been taken in several times, he could not abide the sight of a Daoist. It is just as the saying runs: he who is struck by a fistful of sand from behind goes in fear of the man who follows.

Now Gu Yufeng, seeing Tan Changzhen approaching the manor, called out at the top of his voice, “Master, do not come here to my place! Monks and priests have no affinity with me!” Tan Changzhen cast a look at him, meaning to awaken him; but whether he would receive the teaching — listen to the next chapter for the answer.
If you would have others believe and trust in you, you must first make your own deeds worthy of trust.

blocks.text: 17. Teasing Xihong, He Devises a Plan to Slip Away; Confounding Hunranzi, the Way Is Truly Discussed

inline.s: The mind's own ground must by nature be bright and clear; let not one matter blight a whole life.
Deceived by counterfeit in former years; now that a genuine man appears, he is not recognised.

It is told that Tan Changzhen saw in Gu Yufeng something of a kindly spirit and was minded to awaken him. But Gu Yufeng, not waiting for him to speak, said first, “Master, you need say no more. I have grown weary of hearing such talk as yours. Even if you spoke, I should not believe you. I have been humbugged by your sort until I am afraid of you. Where is there truly a man of practice? As I see it, they are all fellows who merely scheme for food and clothing.” Having spoken, he went within and did not come out again.

Tan Changzhen, hearing these words that made the school of the Way seem wholly without the spirit of the Way, was minded to revive the tradition with all his might. He looked up and saw that night had fallen, so he sat in meditation at the manor gate. When it was fully dark, the farmhands came and pressed him to move on; they carried a bucket of cold water and drenched the gateway, then went back in and shut the door.

Seeing them behave so wickedly, Tan Changzhen did not go to their gate but sat in meditation by the roadside. That night it snowed again, piling up more than a foot deep. At dawn the farmhands came out and saw Changzhen seated in the open courtyard with white snow heaped all about him; yet, strange to tell, not so much as a single flake lay upon his person. They reported this to Yufeng, who came out himself to look. Stepping to his side, he felt a warmth of vital breath greeting him, and knew him for a man of the Way. He thereupon invited him within and treated him with the courtesy due a guest, saying, “It is not that I do not believe in the Way, but that the school of the Way has no good men in it. A venerable elder who practises with such bitter resolve — who would not revere him? I now wish to support you. Stay here in my house three years or five, ten years or eight — it would all please me. Tomorrow I shall choose an auspicious hour and take you for my master; I wonder whether you, venerable elder, will consent?” Tan Changzhen had meant to awaken him, and now saw that he had begun to stir a little faith in the Way, and it was not weak; how could he refuse? So he nodded his assent. Gu Yufeng, overjoyed, ordered a servant to sweep out a room at the rear and invite Tan Changzhen within to sit in contemplation upon the mystery. Each day vegetarian tea and vegetarian meals were provided without stint; and he had the maid Xihong constantly carry broth and water to Tan Changzhen — truly the Way is true and virtue precious, and its subtle principle without end.

Time passed swiftly, and more than half a year went by. He did not see Gu Yufeng come to seek the Way or ask of its principle, and he judged from his intentions that the man loved the Way as a thing to admire rather than to study. He only wished to keep another man supported by his bounty, to have him create merit and do the cultivating on his behalf, while he enjoyed the blessing of good fortune ready-made. Tan Changzhen saw through this device and no longer wished to be supported in the man's house; he repeatedly took his leave and meant to go. But Gu Yufeng pressed him to stay with all his heart, and how would he let him go? He gave orders instead to the members of the household to keep close watch over him. And so, though Changzhen tried to leave several times, they held him back. Since he could not get away, Tan Changzhen thought of a fine stratagem, and concluded that only in this way could he depart. By and by Xihong brought in his tea. Tan Changzhen deliberately pinched her wrist and said, “How white and clean your hand is — enough to make one adore it!” Xihong's cheeks flushed crimson, and she forced herself to answer, “It is white as lacquer; Master, do not tease me.” So saying she went out, straight to the upper chamber, and told the mistress of the Gu household. The wife at once said to her husband, “Master Tan has toyed with our maid; he is no true man of practice and should be sent away.” But Gu Yufeng would not believe it and said, “It is only that Xihong is tired of serving him and so has invented these idle tales.” Seeing her husband speak so, the wife scolded Xihong instead for a while, and Xihong dared say no more.

Two days later, Gu Yufeng, seeing Xihong carry tea to Tan Changzhen, followed behind her to spy for himself. He saw Changzhen clasp Xihong's hand with a winning smile and say, “This hand of yours is white as jade and soft as cotton — it is enough to make one love one to death!” Hearing this from without, Yufeng was greatly angered and meant to turn him out. But then he reflected that the man had often wished to leave and that he himself had repeatedly pressed him to stay; now to expel him would show him unkind. Better to write a few words and paste them on the wall, and let the man see them — if he had any tact, he would surely leave of his own accord. He would only tell the servants not to bar his way; that was a good plan. Leaving Gu Yufeng to his secret preparations, we tell how the next morning Tan Changzhen, having sat until after breakfast and seen neither tea nor water brought by Xihong, knew that his stratagem had taken effect. He went out to look and saw a paper slip pasted on the gate, with four lines written upon it:
All night the west wind drove the flying snow; he sat on the cold mat, his shadow leaning low.
Do not envy the jade-like hand tonight; recall the frog you once were, small and low.

Tan Changzhen read it, smiled to himself, and went into his room. Seeing ink and brush on the table, he took up the brush and came out again, and added four lines of his own to the paper slip. Having written, he went in and gathered his bundle, then ran straight out through the front hall, calling out his thanks twice; no one answered, and he went straight out the manor gate and headed south. He wandered for two years before returning north — but that is to come later, and here we leave it.

Now as for the servants of the Gu household, since their master had given word that when Tan Changzhen came out they need not bar him but let him go of himself, they all drew aside when they saw him come out, and only reported it to their master after he was gone. When he heard of it, Gu Yufeng came to the rear and found four more lines added at the end of the original slip. Which four lines, do you ask?
Say naught of snow and moon and wind-blown flower; an upright heart knows no slanting shadow's power.
Were it not for that jade hand so praised and cried, I'd bide a frog within the well, confined.

Now Gu Yufeng, on seeing these four lines, knew at last that Tan Changzhen's toying with Xihong had been but a stratagem to get away, and he sighed without cease. This tale we set aside to tell of Wang Yuyang, who, after parting from the fellow seekers at Dawei Village, wandered to the region of Fangzhou (present-day Fang County in Hubei). On the northern road of this Fangzhou lived an official surnamed Yao, named Chonggao, who had once been a deputy commander of the New Peace garrison. Having seen through the vanities of the world, he resigned his post and returned home, delighting in the pleasures of field and garden. All his life he was fondest of the Way, and whenever he met a renunciate it was like meeting a kinsman: whether the man had practice or not, he would talk with him awhile. Nearby stood a temple called the Temple of Meeting Immortals. Its abbot too was a Daoist, and monks and priests passing to and fro would often lodge there. He had given the abbot word in advance that whenever a man of genuine practice and virtue came by, word must be brought to him; and the abbot had promised to do so.

One day there came a practitioner who was neither monk nor Daoist, calling himself a man of the Way. He was forever showing off his miraculous powers before people, saying he was ninety-six years old, that he had met Zhang Sanfeng several times and Lu Dongbin on a number of occasions; that Bodhidharma was his master and Jidian his close friend, and that he too could sit in meditation a day or two without once lying down (that is, without sleeping, sitting day and night). That day he arrived at the Temple of Meeting Immortals and spoke of liberating boundless beings. The abbot found his words pleasing and asked his name, and he said his style was Hunranzi. The abbot at once led him to see the honourable Yao. The moment he was presented, he said: “Monks are hungry ghosts in the midst of form, and Daoists are demons of the vital breath; neither can achieve transcendence nor attain Buddhahood. Only if one is like me, able to see through all things and keep the dust of the world from touching him, can he be called a true practitioner. He who learns the Way from me will live several hundred years.”

At these words Yao Chonggao was greatly delighted, and took him for a master, keeping him in his house and providing for him. This old man spoke without the least restraint, belittling monks and Daoists in every sentence. The Daoist of the Temple of Meeting Immortals was present at the time, and hearing him rail against monks and priests felt aggrieved. He thought to himself, “How tactless this old man is! I recommended him in good faith that he might receive support, and he has no regard at all for my dignity, slandering monks and priests to my very face. Does he not know that he who lifts the tiles from the roof should look to the man beneath the eaves? He cares only that the honourable Yao should revere him, and thinks nothing of holding us in contempt. I must find a man who can truly sit in meditation, that this old fellow may be put to shame, and so my heart be satisfied.” Having resolved thus, he took leave of Yao and went back to his temple.

A few days later, as it happened, Wang Yuyang came to lodge there. The abbot, seeing his free and easy bearing, was sure he must be a man of the Way; and seeing that he sat in meditation all day with a clear and vigorous spirit, judged that if any man might refute the old fellow, it would have to be this one. He wished to explain the matter to him but feared he would not go. So he hit upon a plan and said to Yuyang, “A great practitioner has come to the household of the honourable Yao, one who can sit more than ten days without once lying down. I should like to go with my fellow seeker and pay him a visit; what do you think of it?” Wang Yuyang was delighted to hear it, and went with the abbot to the Yao mansion. The gatekeeper went in and announced them, and Yao Chonggao came out himself to welcome them and brought them to the reception hall to take tea.
Before they could begin to talk, a white-haired old man came in. Wang Yuyang looked at him: the fellow had coarse brows and narrow eyes, an upturned nose, and high cheekbones (
quán

), with his lips and teeth thrust forward. Square of face and long of ear, he trailed a few wispy beard-hairs and showed a scant scattering of white hair on his head, so that he looked like an old crone. He came in and sat down in the seat of honour. The abbot said to Wang Yuyang, “This venerable gentleman is the great practitioner of whom I spoke.” At this Wang Yuyang stepped forward to make his salutation. The old man sat there quite unmoved, holding Yuyang in no esteem whatever, and said, “Tell me, fellow seeker — did you plant a flower, or did you plant a willow?” Wang Yuyang was wholly at a loss and did not answer. The old man asked again, “Have you a wife?” Wang Yuyang thought his questions merely vulgar and so answered offhand, “I do have a wife, but she is left at home, parted from me now.” Hunranzi gave a great guffaw and said, “You have left home for nothing! You do not know even so much. Let me teach you: “to plant a flower” is to leave home while young; “to plant a willow” is to leave home in middle age. When I asked whether you had a wife, I meant, have you come by the tidings of the true yin? You answered me in worldly speech, which shows you do not understand. And if I asked you of “conceiving a child,” you would know even less!”

Though Hunranzi insulted a man to his face, Wang Yuyang did not take it to heart; but how could the abbot's face keep its colour? Seeing the abbot flush crimson with shame, Yuyang could not but argue a little, that the dignity of all present might be saved. So he smiled and asked, “Just now the venerable gentleman spoke of the “true yin” — what thing precisely is the true yin? He spoke too of “conceiving a child”; but I know not in what place the child is conceived, nor what it is that is carried.” Hunranzi could not for the moment answer, and forced a smile, saying, “The mysterious mechanism may not be divulged; how could I lightly speak of it with the likes of you?” The abbot, seeing the old man force these words and knowing he was ignorant, said to Wang Yuyang, “Pray go on and speak, fellow seeker; I judge he knows nothing. There is no need to ask him.” But what was it that Wang Yuyang said? Hear the next chapter for the answer.
Oft he boasted in mighty terms; at a single question, no reply.

blocks.text: 18. Wang Yuyang, With the True, Subdues the False; Tan Changzhen, Telling of the Past, Warrants the Present

inline.s: They tell that in the Western Land a lotus rare is sown; blooms ten fathoms high, the root-stock like a boat is grown.
The mind's own altar bears the Jetavana tree; this very ground is Buddha's heaven to see.

It is told that with a few essential words Wang Yuyang refuted Hunranzi, so that he could not answer. The abbot, standing by, clapped his hands and laughed aloud, urging Yuyang to go on and speak and not be hard on the man, for he judged that he could not know it. Hunranzi, seeing the abbot say he knew nothing, began to take offence; but Wang Yuyang at once explained, “It is not that the venerable gentleman does not know — it is that he is unwilling to speak! Let me presume to set forth the principle, that we all may weigh it and see whether it be so. The “true yin” and the “true yang” are the two breaths of yin and yang. The true yang breath is stored in the liver, and the true yin breath is gathered in the lungs. The liver is wood, the dwelling of the soul; the lungs are metal, the abode of the earthly spirit. Metal is the Dui maiden and wood the Zhen youth; wood flourishes in the east and metal is born in the west. Therefore one likens them to the young man of the eastern house and the maiden of the western house. Now would one make metal and wood meet — the soul never leaving the earthly spirit, the earthly spirit never leaving the soul, as a husband cleaves to his wife and a wife to her husband — this is the principle of the union of yin and yang, and it is exactly what the venerable Hunranzi meant when he asked me whether I had a household. Yet one must borrow the Yellow Matron to lure them into meeting before they can see each other. The Yellow Matron is the true intention: by intention one accords with intention, and then metal and wood are both without separation, and so they attain the harmony of husband and wife. Intention belongs to earth and is full of feeling; its colour is yellow and it is fond of motion, whence it is likened to an old woman. Coming and going between east and west, it brings the two houses into communication, just like a matchmaker. As for “conceiving a child,” it is to say that the true breath congeals within the lower elixir field, as though with child. When the true breath is complete it manifests in spirit, and so it is said that spirit is the child of breath and breath the mother of spirit; hence comes the talk of the descent of the infant. When one reaches this point, the great elixir is accomplished, and one may grow old together with Heaven and Earth and share the rest of sun and moon.”

When the honourable Yao heard these words, his praise knew no end. Hunranzi, fearing that Wang Yuyang would snatch the rice-bowl from him, said grandly, “He who has virtue must have words, but he who has words need not have virtue. If you dare to sit in meditation with me and go two or three days without touching tea or water, then you may be said to have attainment.” Wang Yuyang smiled and said, “For longer than that, this humble one cannot sit; but two or three days — I am glad to keep you company.” Thereupon the two began to vie in the practice.

They spread felt and padded mats in the reception hall and sat side by side. Hunranzi had naturally been able to sit two or three days without tea or water; but because he was to be tested against Yuyang, a spark of resentment had lodged in his heart, and this made him unable to sit in peace and bred troubles without end. At one moment he thought of asking for tea, at the next he must go out and relieve himself, so that in a single day he left his seat several times. By the second day he could sit no longer, and actually got down from the mat to seek food and drink, and fell into a doze, snoring thunderously. Wang Yuyang sat on resolutely until the third day before he left his seat, and then felt all the clearer and brisker of spirit for it.

The honourable Yao praised him repeatedly, saying, “Master, in the art of sitting the venerable gentleman is no match for you.” Wang Yuyang said, “It is not that the venerable gentleman is inferior to me; it is that his years are advanced, and in old age the breath weakens. Were I at his age, I fear I could not endure half a day.” When Hunranzi heard this, he was won over in his heart, and came again to talk with him; he no longer dared hold himself high and mighty, but by degrees grew humble and lowly.

Wang Yuyang stayed several days in the Yao household, and taught him a few sections of the dark work of cultivation, and the two were greatly taken with each other. One day Yuyang excused himself on the pretence of going to the Temple of Meeting Immortals to fetch his baggage, but once gone he did not return for several days. Yao Chonggao sent a servant to ask, and the abbot said he had left that very day. When the honourable Yao heard this he stamped his foot and sighed deeply, saying their affinity was thin. Even Hunranzi was somewhat loath to see him go.

Setting aside the matter of Wang Yuyang, we tell of Liu Changsheng, who after parting from his fellow seekers made a journey south and then went again to eastern Lu, where he cultivated with whole-hearted devotion on Mount Tai for three years, and so attained the true fruit. He ascended to the upper realm, was feasted in the Jasper Pool, and went to pay homage to the Queen Mother. He saw behind her a host of dozens of celestial maidens thronging together, of a beauty rare in the world, past all depiction and description, both lovely and to be longed for. Unable to check the stirring of a single thought, he stole a glance at the assembled maidens. The Queen Mother asked, “You gaze upon them — what is your intention?” Hearing the Queen Mother's words, Liu Changsheng knew he had transgressed propriety, and in trepidation begged pardon, prostrating himself and saying, “Your subject chanced to see the rainbow garments swirling and the bright sleeves outstretched, and in a moment of inadvertence cast a glance at the celestial maidens. In truth I had no other intent; I beseech your gracious countenance to forgive me.”

The Queen Mother reproved him, saying, “The distinction of self and other is still within you, and the marks of form are yet not emptied. Even if you have perfected the golden elixir, you cannot rise beyond the ordinary and enter the sacred. Descend once more to the mortal world and cultivate with bitter toil.” Thereupon she ordered a celestial official to escort him down. The official of the Southern Heaven, obeying the Queen Mother's command, led Liu Changsheng to the Southern Heaven Gate. Just as Changsheng was about to ride the clouds downward, the official had already given him a shove in the back, and he tumbled from the Southern Heaven Gate. Of a sudden he woke and knew it had all been a dream and an illusion. When he recalled the affair of the Jasper Pool, it was truly the fault of a single thought. And the Master Chongyang had once said of him: “In the elixir arts you excel in all things; only in the marks of form are you not yet empty.” Now that in his dream he had entered the Jasper Pool and heard the Queen Mother's reproof, it tallied exactly with the Master's words. But how was this task of cultivation to be done? He must descend the mountain and seek out a man of eminence to instruct him.

So he came down the mountain, and after travelling but a few days he met Tan Changzhen, and the two told each other of all that had befallen them. Liu Changsheng said, “Your refusal to be supported by the Gu household was no unrighteous thought; but my mistakingly gazing upon the celestial maiden at the Jasper Pool was no small error. Now I wish to cultivate emptiness of the marks of form, but I do not know where to begin.” Tan Changzhen said, “In the days of old, when Xu Jingyang was young, he was devoted to the chase. One day, hunting among the mountains, he let an arrow fly at a fawn. With the arrow in its body the fawn fled, and Jingyang led his family over the whole mountain in search of it, until he found two deer in a hollow. The fawn lay on the ground and the doe lay licking its wound. When the doe saw men come, she did not flee either, and both were captured. When they were taken home and unbound, both deer were already dead; and when their bellies were opened, the doe's bowels were found broken into inch-long pieces, while the fawn, though wounded, had its bowels quite whole. From this one may see that a mother's grief for her young is sharper far than the pain of the arrow itself. Seeing this, Jingyang's heart was stirred to pity; he broke up his bow and arrows, went into the mountains to cultivate, and so attained the true fruit. Wishing to convert and deliver all beings in the ten directions, he ascended a platform to proclaim the Dharma and gathered several hundred disciples.”

One day Jingyang said to his disciples, “You several hundred are not few in number, and your abandonment of home to study the Way is not lacking in devotion. But a man of practice must see through the marks of form. Can you look upon beauty without greed?” The disciples answered with one voice, “As for wealth, and anger, and wine, we may not have cast them all away; but as for the matter of lust, we have always taken it lightly and are not greedy for it.” Xu Jingyang said, “You speak so cleanly — I only fear it may not be so.” The disciples answered, “How would we dare speak falsely to deceive our master?” Xu Jingyang said, “I have a method that will test the truth of it. Let each of you prepare a piece of charcoal, more than two feet long, or three or four feet if you can, and set it on your bed to sleep with you for a night. When you rise tomorrow morning, bring it to me. Then if you have genuine attainment, I will transmit it to you.” The disciples, hearing this and not knowing the reason, each went to prepare a piece of charcoal and placed it on his bed.

That night, a disciple woke from his slumbers to find another sleeping beside him. When he reached out a hand and touched it, it was warm and soft as cotton, smooth as jade. Feeling further down the body, he found it was a woman. His desire blazed up suddenly and could not be curbed, and he gave himself over to it. Once his true yang had been shed, he still clung to her fondly and slept in her embrace. At dawn voices called from outside, “Bring the charcoal, come quickly — the master has been waiting a long while!” The disciples started from their dreams, and every one of them was holding a piece of charcoal in his arms. Just as they were wondering at this, the voices called again, and they could only dress and come to hand over their charcoal. Jingyang bade the disciples stand in two rows and come up one after another to present it. The disciples dared not disobey, so they stood in two rows, and one came forward to present his charcoal. Xu Jingyang asked, “How old are you?” The man said, “Your disciple is this year seventy-six.” Jingyang said, “At so great an age, why can you not see through the matter of lust?” The man answered, “How does your disciple appear not to see through it?” Jingyang said, “Since you can see through the matter of lust, then what is that which is smeared on your charcoal?” The man looked at his charcoal, and midway along it saw some faint white spots, the marks of a defilement. Only then did he realise it was the true yang he had shed the night before; feeling ashamed, he hung his head and dared not make a sound. Only then did the others understand that the woman with whom they had lain that night had been a transformation of the charcoal. When they looked at their own charcoal again, there were even more marks upon it. Afraid of being shamed before the rest, each stood frozen and would not bring up his charcoal; though urged again and again, none would stir. Only one man stepped forward smiling, and presented his charcoal with no trace upon it at all. Xu Jingyang asked, “Lust is what men delight in — why is it you do not care for it?” The man answered, “Your disciple has cultivated it out of the midst of lust itself.” Jingyang asked how he had done so, and he said, “Whatever one delights in, one must also fear. At first one fears he cannot get it; but once it is in hand, then from morning to night he takes his pleasure and will not stop. When a man is worn in spirit and weak in breath, and moreover frets over life and death, this is what makes him fear. When fear grows great he must flee from it, and so, meeting the object of his desire, he forgets his longing, and cuts off desire to preserve his life. In my youth I was dissolute and unrestrained, lying among the flowers and sleeping among the willows all day, and for a whole year I never went home. I made the house of pleasure my own home, and saw many beautiful dames and ladies, and tasted endless moons of pleasure and flowers of wanton bliss, until my spirit was wounded. I grew afraid and wished to flee, but could not escape; and so I fled here and studied the Way, wishing to preserve my life and no longer cling to beauty. There is no other trick in it than this, that having seen and known much, and having gone through it, one lets it go.” Xu Jingyang nodded at these words, and sent all the other disciples away, keeping only this one, to whom he transmitted the mystery of the Way; and in the end he too attained the true fruit. Judging from this, in all matters one must have seen and known much before the heart can hold them lightly and let them go.

When Tan Changzhen had finished this tale of the ancients, Liu Changsheng said, “I never had a mind for the inner practice; it was only that I delighted in their outward beauty. Some day I shall go to the house of pleasure and survey all the painted brows and powdered faces, until I have gained breadth of knowledge and experience, and my eyes are open and wide.” Tan Changzhen invited him to go to the region of Jin and see the birthplace of the Ancestor of the Way.

The two travelled on for many days, and on the way met Wang Yuyang, and the three went on together. Yuyang then told the two of the discourse on the Way he had had with Hunranzi at the Yao household. Liu Changsheng laughed and said, “It was cheap gain for that old fellow — the mystery of our Way was won by him.” Wang Yuyang said, “If I had not been able to sit in meditation, the old man would never have been convinced.” Tan Changzhen said, “So it seems. The practice of sitting is the staff that knocks at the gate for all who study the Way; whoever is of our school must learn it.” As the three walked and talked, they suddenly heard someone behind crying out, “How fast you have gone!” Who was this person? We must look to the next chapter to know.
